PTHA18 · from-scratch run report

Alaska, Built From Scratch

A full run through 32,000 logic-tree branches for the Alaska subduction interface, using only public data: SLAB1.0 geometry, Bird (2003) convergence, and a fresh GCMT catalogue subset. This report reads back what each of the seven build steps actually wrote to disk.

UNSEGMENTED RUN. The zone is one fault that can break from end to end, with weight 1 (no LEVEL 0 segments), so every curve and number on this page is the zone's. A segmented run of the same zone (generate.py ... --segmented true) adds a LEVEL 0 section and mixes this answer 50/50 with the sum of its segments.

Step by step

What each script did, and the real numbers it produced on this run.

STEP 1-2 Interface geometry from an external meshgiven

This run does not build its mesh from SLAB: it uses the quadrilateral mesh in inputs/geometry/alaskaaleutians_quadrilateral_coors.dat, one line per unit source with its four corners (lon, lat, depth), read by pyptha/mesh_file.py (rows, columns and orientation found from the corners the cells share) and used as given. Everything from step 3 on is computed on it exactly as on a SLAB mesh.

STEP 1 Interface geometry from SLAB1.0derived

Downloaded depth contours for the Alaska region from SLAB1.0 (Hayes, Wald & Johnson 2012, USGS), unwrapped the antimeridian crossing if needed, and clipped to this zone's own seismogenic cutoff, derived from Berryman et al. (2015).

Contours kept—

STEP 2 Unit-source gridderived

Took the unit sources from the external mesh, as given, and computed per-unit-source statistics: length, width, dip, strike, depth.

No official unit_source_statistics_alaskaaleutians.nc found. Run step8_official.py first (needs R with rptha installed) for the official mesh map and the two comparison figures.

STEP 2 The mesh on a real mapcheck by eye

The mesh is a real place on Earth, so it must sit where the real subduction zone is. The background is Esri's ocean map, which shades the sea floor by its depth: the trench is the long, narrow, dark groove where one plate bends down under the other. The thick line of each mesh is its top edge (its shallowest cells) and should run along that groove; from there the mesh follows the sinking plate down, under the island arc, to step 1's depth limit. Drag to move, zoom with the buttons or a double click (the mouse wheel zooms after a click on the map), and change the background or hide a mesh in the box at the top right.

This map needs an internet connection: it loads the Leaflet map library and Esri's map tiles.
this run: 312 cells (thick line: top edge)

Unlike the rest of this report, this map is not stored in the page: the Leaflet map library and Esri's tiles load from the internet when the page opens. PTHA18's published cell outlines could not be read for this zone, so only this run's mesh is drawn.

STEP 3 Convergence from Bird (2003)derived

Matched the top edge of every along-strike column to its nearest Bird (2003) plate-boundary segment and area-weighted the convergent velocities, exactly as PTHA18 does (on PTHA18's own mesh this gives the official value to machine precision). The number below is horizontal plate motion; step 7 divides it by cos(mean dip), once, to get slip on the inclined fault plane. The per-column values also set how likely each rupture is (faster convergence under it, higher probability) and the shape the LEVEL 4 edge fit aims for, as in PTHA18.

This run55.35 mm/yr

STEP 4 GCMT catalogue downloadderived

Downloaded the worldwide Global CMT catalogue from 1976-01-01 to 2017-03-01, parsed from the raw NDK record format. This matches PTHA18's own observation window exactly (report Section 3.7.3), so the event counts are directly comparable with the official run.

Events, worldwide47,689
Window1976-01-01 – 2017-03-01

STEP 5 GCMT subset for this zonederived

Applied a from-scratch reimplementation of gcmt_subsetter.R: hypocentre OR centroid within 0.4° of a unit source, either nodal plane thrust-like (within 50° of pure dip-slip) and strike-aligned with the unit source nearest the CENTROID (within 50°), depth ≤71 km, Mw≥7.15, over 1976-01-01 – 2017-03-01 (PTHA18's own window, report Section 3.7.3).

STEP 6 Assemble the input JSONpartly declared

Combined the derived geometry, convergence and seismicity with three literature values that cannot be derived from geometry or a catalogue: seismic coupling (cmin/cpref/cmax = 0.42/0.55/0.77), the b-value anchor, and the largest historically observed magnitude (Mw 9.2, the larger of Berryman's largest row and step 5's largest event) -- all from Berryman et al. (2015)'s "GEM Faulted Earth Subduction Interface Characterisation Project" via berryman_params.py (coupling from its Whole Margin row where it has one), not from any PTHA18-internal file.

STEP 7 Run LEVELs 0–5derived

Enumerated the full logic tree, solved the moment balance for each branch's Gutenberg-Richter 'a' parameter, applied the Bayesian update from step 5's observations, fitted the along-strike edge taper, and sampled percentiles.

Branches32,000
GR 'a' range2.79 – 8.75
Edge multiplier1.08
Prior→posterior shift0.531 TVD
What the Bayesian update did here Total variation distance between prior and posterior is 0.53 (0 = no change, 1 = complete reshuffle). With 5 observed event(s) pulling toward specific branches, that is how much LEVEL 3 moved the weights — run step8_official.py to compare this against the official update's shift.

LEVEL 2: rupture generationFAUS

Before any rate is computed, every branch needs an actual set of earthquake-sized ruptures to assign rates to. For each magnitude in the 7.2–9.8 range (step 0.1), pyptha_v12/events.py (a port of rptha's rupture_events.R) sizes a rectangular block of unit sources from the Strasser scaling relation and enumerates every valid placement of that block on the mesh -- each placement is one rupture, with uniform slip set so its seismic moment matches M0(Mw) exactly. This is the FAUS (Fixed Area Uniform Slip) rupture type, and every LEVEL 0–5 rate number on this page is computed from FAUS ruptures only. This run used --rupture-size local (v10, not PTHA18's procedure): the block size is chosen again at every placement from the real km of the cells there, so the rupture area follows the scaling relation even where the cells differ a lot in size; a magnitude's ruptures can then have different numbers of cells. v10_q: each rupture's conditional probability is also multiplied by q, the mean over its cells of 1 / (number of ruptures of that magnitude containing the cell), so that places covered by more ruptures (smaller cells) do not get more rate for the same area and convergence.

Total ruptures enumerated3,851
Magnitude range7.2 – 9.8

FAUS (the rupture the rates use) VAUS both

VAUS: step 7b's variable-area uniform-slip fields drawn from the FAUS rupture shown. Each carries a share of that rupture's rate (PTHA18's rule, shown on its line); none of it enters LEVELs 0-5. Play steps through the FAUS ruptures; the VAUS menu picks the realisation.

The scaling relation (Strasser) gives, for each Mw, a median rupture area (1 on this axis). Real earthquakes of the same Mw scatter around it by about a factor of 2: ±1σ is 0.50 to 2.01 times that area (shaded), and about 1 in 3 earthquakes falls outside that range.

VAUS: for each realisation, PTHA18 (and step 7b) draws a rupture length and a width separately from Strasser's own scatter, cut at ±2σ (length 0.44 to 2.29 times the median, width 0.45 to 2.22), makes the heterogeneous slip in that rectangle, and the VAUS is the rectangle around the cells that slipped. So VAUS areas spread like real earthquakes, and fall lower where the edge of the zone cuts the rectangle.

Small dots: every FAUS rupture of this Mw, and every VAUS realisation of the FAUS rupture shown; hollow: a VAUS above PTHA18's peak-slip limit (rate 0). Large dots: the ones on the map. Log scale.

Same moment for every rupture of this Mw, so a smaller area means a larger slip. Black dashed: the slip the median area gives (); shaded: the slip for the ±1σ areas.

Red: PTHA18's peak-slip limit, 7.5 times that slip (). PTHA18 gives an HS or VAUS scenario above it rate 0 (config_peak_slip_limit_factor.R), and so does step 7b (v10_q); hollow dots are those. FAUS is never limited. Log scale.

STEP 7b Heterogeneous-slip (HS) and variable-area-uniform-slip (VAUS)rates shared from FAUS, not in LEVELs 0-5

pyptha_v12/stochastic_slip.py (a port of rptha's SFFM generator, the SNCF method of Davies et al. 2015) turns each FAUS rupture into a heterogeneous-slip realisation: same total slip (and hence the same Mw) as the FAUS rupture, but concentrated into asperities instead of spread uniformly. This covers EVERY magnitude this run generated FAUS ruptures for (27 magnitude(s)) and, for each one, up to 4395 of that magnitude's real FAUS placements (LEVEL 2 above enumerates every valid one -- see "Total ruptures enumerated") -- 58,022 HS field(s) in total, summarised by magnitude below; the underlying summary.csv has one row PER FIELD (not a sample), with the field's own full footprint kept as event_index_string/event_slip_string, rptha's own packed format. None of this feeds into the logic tree -- every rate number in this report, including the exceedance-rate curve below, is FAUS-only, exactly as PTHA18 itself computes LEVELs 0–5. HS here is an illustrative addition (more realistic tsunami initial conditions), not an alternative rate model.

Rates (v10_q). Each HS field, and each VAUS field, takes a share of the rate of the FAUS rupture it was drawn from, as PTHA18 does (compute_rates_all_sources.R 1551–1600, ported in pyptha_v12/hs_vaus_rates.py): a field whose peak slip is above 7.5 times the scaling relation's mean slip for its Mw gets rate 0; the others are weighted by the rank of their peak slip among the fields of the same FAUS rupture, with PTHA18's DART-calibrated weights (recovered from its published HS/VAUS rates, which they reproduce to 1e-12), and the shares of one FAUS rupture add up to 1. The rates are in the two summary.csv files; they enter nothing in LEVELs 0–5 or in the rate curve.

VAUS (Variable Area Uniform Slip), derived from the HS fields above

rptha does not generate VAUS independently -- it derives it from the ALREADY-GENERATED HS table (make_all_earthquake_events.R lines ~255–345): same Mw, target location and peak-slip cell as the matching HS field, but with slip spread uniformly over the smallest rectangle that contains the HS field's own footprint, at whatever single slip value keeps sum(slip×area) -- and hence Mw -- unchanged. This step reproduces that exact derivation for every HS field generated above: 58,022 VAUS field(s) in total, one per HS field, summarised by magnitude below.

STEP 7c Shear modulus: constant30 GPa

Every rate on this page uses a constant rigidity (shear modulus) of 30 GPa, as PTHA18's rate_annual, the rates compared with PTHA18 throughout this report. PTHA18 also publishes rates with a rigidity that grows with depth (variable_mu_rate_annual); this pipeline computes them in step 7c when the example is generated with --variable-mu on (from_scratch_v12), which was not done here.

Every one of the 32,000 logic-tree branches' own Mw-vs-exceedance-rate curve (grey), before the Bayesian update (left) and after it (right), against the 5 observed event(s) from step 5 (green). This is the engine's own figure, produced in step 7/8, not redrawn for this report.

Observed events5

What the moment-balance “target” actually is

Added up over every scenario, the slip the earthquakes release along the zone should have the same shape as the plate convergence: that shape is LEVEL 4's target. Here it is Bird's convergent rate of each column (convergence_profile in the input JSON), as in PTHA18. Near the two ends of the zone fewer scenarios overlap, so the released slip sags there (grey). LEVEL 4 fits a single multiplier of the probability of scenarios that touch an end (1.078 on this run) until the two shapes agree as well as possible (orange). The three curves are normalised to the same total, because only the shapes are compared; one multiplier can lift the ends but cannot reshape the middle.

no edge correctiontarget: plate convergence shapeedge-corrected
